However in the absence of strong move to enter into production it will be forced to revoke any idle oil blocks and recover assets from operators who have failed to commence development within stipulated timelines.
The directive is coming as indigenous firm Heirs Energies doubles effort to bring idle wells into compliance.
The Commission also urged holders of Petroleum Prospecting Licences (PPLs) to move swiftly from award to production, warning against the historical pattern of licences sitting idle.
With this renewed support, the NUPRC expects the 22 awardees to contribute at least 250,000 barrels of oil per day to national production.
The Commission Chief Executive, NUPRC, Mrs. Oritsemeyiwa Eyesan, stated this while speaking in Lagos at the NUPRC Onboarding Workshop for PPL holders themed “From Award to Production: Delivering Nigeria’s Upstream Petroleum Potential under the Petroleum Industry Act, 2021.
”Eyesan said the two-day workshop was designed to prevent early mistakes that stalled previous bid rounds, stressing that it is also part of efforts to translate recent awards into reserves growth and production, in line with the PIA 2021 objective of unlocking Nigeria’s upstream potential.
“For this set of awardees, we are expecting nothing less than 250,000 barrels per day in the next five years at least from the 22 awards,” Eyesan said, adding that Nigeria remains on course to hit 3MMBOPD by 2030.
She welcomed participants from the 2020, 2022/2023 and 2024 licensing rounds, noting that with licence instruments now issued, operators must “hit the ground running” but in a structured, compliant way.
Eyesan said the Commission convened the workshop after reviewing past licensing cycles where many awardees struggled to progress. “We had post-award challenges. Most sat on their acreages,” she said. “Even marginal fields didn’t quite take off.
”Drawing from industry experience, she noted that in the 2010/2012 divestment rounds, some operators who understood the business took zero-production assets to 60,000 bpd, and brownfields to 80,000 bpd, while others failed to set up proper upstream structures despite meeting financial obligations.
According to her, “Oil and gas is a specialized business. Some paid the signature bonus but failed in setting up the business,” she said, recalling an operator whose accounts were not even on an Excel sheet.
Eyesan said the Commission’s role under the PIA is not just regulatory but enabling, to ensure awardees understand obligations and how to engage the regulator.“Over the next two days we will walk you through the entire journey — what are your work programme, technical and host community obligations, when and how to approach the Commission, and what support we provide,” she said.
She urged participants to use the platform to network and build industry collaboration, referencing how trade groups like the IPPG have helped members benchmark and share best practices to drive competitiveness.
The first day of the onboarding programme was attended by subject matter experts from the Commission as well as several notable professionals from legal and financial institutions who provided first-hand knowledge to the new awardees.
The first day of the workshop covered five technical sessions from award of licence to production of first oil. Focus areas included regulatory framework, work programme, exploration, appraisal and commerciality, field development, well operations and production as well as exploration financing.
Eyesan advised the new awardees to learn from the successes and mistakes of past winners.
She restated the October 31, 2026 deadline for the revocation of idle oil and gas licences in line with the drill-or-drop provision enshrined in the Petroleum Industry Act.
Eyesan added, “We have issued a directive that by the end of this month, those who were awarded licences and have not done anything within the stipulated time — three years for those onshore and five years for those offshore — the Commission will call in those blocks. It’s going to be drill or drop.
This is standard practice all over the world. In the UK, in the Netherlands, all over the world.”The Chief Executive noted that such extensions would no longer be granted automatically.
“We want to see that in the next two years, more than half of you have reached first oil. In the next three, four years, you are drilling your second well.”
Meanwhile Heirs Energies technical team in compliance with government’s regulations would be showcasing its strategies for restoring underperforming oil and gas wells and improving asset performance at the Upstream Production Optimisation & Asset Performance Summit 2026, scheduled to hold in Lagos on Wednesday, October 21.
The company said two of its technical leaders, Deputy Vice President, Engineering, Sunny Adoga, and Senior Reservoir Engineer, Cleverson Esene, would join industry experts to discuss practical solutions to challenges constraining Nigeria’s upstream petroleum production.
Adoga is expected to participate in a panel session titled, “Silent Wells, Lost Barrels: Bringing Declining and Shut-In Wells Back Stronger,” where he will share strategies for reviving underperforming wells and improving production efficiency.
Esene will participate in another panel, “Follow the Barrel: Where Is Nigeria’s Production Being Held Back?”, examining factors limiting the country’s oil and gas output and opportunities to unlock additional value from existing assets.
The summit will take place at the Lagos Oriental Hotel, bringing together upstream operators, regulators, engineering companies and technology providers to explore ways of increasing production, reducing operational downtime and improving asset performance.
Heirs Energies said its contributions would draw on its operational experience at Oil Mining Lease (OML) 17 in the Niger Delta, where targeted interventions have helped improve production from a mature asset.
The company’s participation comes as Nigeria intensifies efforts to recover shut-in production, reduce output losses and maximise the value of existing oil and gas infrastructure.
In January 2026, the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC) identified production optimisation and revenue expansion as key priorities for the country’s upstream sector, emphasising the need to restore economically viable shut-in wells, arrest production decline and accelerate the delivery of new production.
The commission also highlighted regulatory efficiency, infrastructure integrity and improved hydrocarbon measurement as critical to increasing national output.
In October, the NUPRC announced that more than 788,000 barrels per day of shut-in production had been identified across 63 operators, underscoring the scale of the opportunity to recover lost output from existing assets.
Against this backdrop, technical discussions at the summit are expected to focus on practical interventions that can help operators overcome production constraints without relying exclusively on expensive new developments
